children.topic: HPD 500 · Paediatrics and Child Health II
children.note: Clinical paediatrics for the Kenyan hospital: neonatal emergencies, pneumonia, diarrhoea, malnutrition, malaria, HIV, TB, sickle cell, heart and kidney disease and childhood cancers, using the Basic Paediatric Protocols.

children.note: Four main groups plus eclampsia and HELLP.
BP ≥140/90 mmHg before pregnancy or diagnosed before 20 weeks' gestation.

manas.q: How is chronic hypertension in pregnancy defined?

children.note: New BP ≥140/90 at or after 20 weeks with no proteinuria or other pre-eclampsia features.

manas.q: How is gestational hypertension defined?

children.note: Urine protein:creatinine ratio ≥30 mg/mmol or ≥300 mg in 24 hours; dipstick 2+ if quantification unavailable.

manas.q: What proteinuria thresholds support a diagnosis of pre-eclampsia?

children.note: Chronic hypertension plus new proteinuria, organ dysfunction or uteroplacental dysfunction after 20 weeks.

manas.q: What is superimposed pre-eclampsia?

children.note: New generalised tonic-clonic seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia, with no other cause found.

manas.q: How is eclampsia defined?

children.note: HELLP may appear with only mild, or even absent, hypertension or proteinuria; check bloods in any unwell woman.

manas.q: Can HELLP syndrome occur without marked hypertension?

children.note: Early-onset (<34 weeks) is more placental and severe, with more growth restriction; late-onset (≥34 weeks) is commoner.

manas.q: How do early-onset and late-onset pre-eclampsia differ?

children.note: A two-stage disease: placenta first, mother second.
Shallow trophoblast invasion fails to remodel spiral arteries, leaving narrow, high-resistance vessels and an underperfused placenta.

manas.q: What goes wrong with the spiral arteries in pre-eclampsia?

children.note: The stressed placenta releases sFlt-1 and soluble endoglin, which bind and lower free PlGF and VEGF.

manas.q: Which angiogenic factors are altered in pre-eclampsia?

children.note: Widespread maternal endothelial damage causes vasoconstriction, capillary leak, platelet activation and organ injury.

manas.q: What is the maternal stage of pre-eclampsia?

children.note: Kidney (glomerular endotheliosis), liver (periportal injury, capsule stretch), brain (oedema, PRES), clotting and lungs.

manas.q: Which organs are affected in pre-eclampsia and how?

children.note: NICE groups them into high and moderate risk.
Previous hypertensive pregnancy, chronic kidney disease, SLE or antiphospholipid syndrome, type 1 or 2 diabetes, chronic hypertension.

manas.q: Name the NICE high-risk factors for pre-eclampsia.

children.note: First pregnancy, age ≥40, interval >10 years, BMI ≥35 at booking, family history of pre-eclampsia, multiple pregnancy.

manas.q: Name the NICE moderate-risk factors for pre-eclampsia.

children.note: One high-risk factor, or two or more moderate-risk factors.

manas.q: Which women qualify for aspirin prophylaxis under NICE?

children.note: Pre-eclampsia before 20 weeks suggests molar pregnancy (or triploidy); scan the uterus.

manas.q: What should pre-eclampsia before 20 weeks make you suspect?

children.note: Signs that pre-eclampsia is severe (ACOG and NICE features combined).
Severe persistent headache, visual disturbance (flashing lights, blurring), epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, vomiting.

manas.q: Which symptoms suggest severe pre-eclampsia?

children.note: BP ≥160/110, brisk reflexes with clonus, papilloedema, pulmonary oedema, low urine output.

manas.q: Which signs suggest severe pre-eclampsia?

children.note: Platelets <100 × 10⁹/L, transaminases twice normal or more, rising creatinine.

manas.q: Which laboratory results indicate severe pre-eclampsia?

children.note: The amount of proteinuria no longer defines severity in ACOG or NICE guidance.

manas.q: Does heavy proteinuria define severe pre-eclampsia?

children.note: Mother and fetus both need assessment.
Seated, correct cuff size, arm at heart level; use Korotkoff phase V for diastolic.

manas.q: Which Korotkoff sound marks diastolic BP in pregnancy?

children.note: FBC (platelets), U&E and creatinine, LFTs; add LDH and blood film for haemolysis, and clotting if platelets are low.

manas.q: Which blood tests are done in suspected pre-eclampsia?

children.note: Dipstick screen, then quantify with protein:creatinine ratio.

manas.q: How is proteinuria quantified in pregnancy?

children.note: Ultrasound for growth and liquor, umbilical artery Doppler, and CTG.

manas.q: How is the fetus assessed in pre-eclampsia?

children.note: Low PlGF or a high sFlt-1/PlGF ratio supports pre-eclampsia; a normal ratio helps rule it out in the short term.

manas.q: How does PlGF-based testing help in suspected pre-eclampsia?

children.note: Control BP to protect the mother, mainly from stroke.
Labetalol (avoid in asthma), nifedipine (oral, modified or immediate release, not sublingual), methyldopa.

manas.q: Which oral antihypertensives are used in pregnancy?

children.note: Treat ≥160/110 urgently, within 30–60 min, with oral nifedipine, IV labetalol or IV hydralazine; avoid sudden falls.

manas.q: How quickly should severe hypertension in pregnancy be treated?

children.note: NICE aims for about 135/85 mmHg once on treatment.

manas.q: What BP target does NICE use for treated hypertension in pregnancy?

children.note: ACE inhibitors and ARBs (fetal renal harm), and atenolol (growth restriction); diuretics are not routine.

manas.q: Which antihypertensives should be avoided in pregnancy?

children.note: The CHAP trial (2022) found treating mild chronic hypertension to <140/90 improved pregnancy outcomes.

manas.q: What did the CHAP trial show about mild chronic hypertension in pregnancy?

children.note: Drug of choice to prevent and treat eclampsia.
Eclampsia, and severe pre-eclampsia to prevent fits; continue for 24 hours after delivery or the last fit.

manas.q: When is magnesium sulphate given in pre-eclampsia?

children.note: Loading 4 g IV slowly, then a 1 g/hour IV infusion for 24 hours.

manas.q: What is the Zuspan regimen of magnesium sulphate?

children.note: Pritchard: 4 g IV plus 10 g IM (5 g each buttock), then 5 g IM 4-hourly; no pump needed. Zuspan needs a controlled IV infusion but avoids painful IM injections.

manas.q: What practical difference is there between Pritchard and Zuspan regimens?

children.note: Give a further 2 g IV slowly, then continue maintenance.

manas.q: What is given if a woman fits again on magnesium sulphate?

children.note: Check reflexes, breathing rate and urine output regularly; magnesium is renally cleared, so reduce or stop in oliguria.

manas.q: Why must magnesium dosing be reviewed in oliguria?

children.note: Magpie trial: more than halved eclampsia risk. It beats diazepam and phenytoin for treating eclampsia.

manas.q: Which trial showed magnesium sulphate prevents eclampsia?

children.note: Delivery cures; timing balances mother against fetus.
Gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia without severe features: plan birth at 37 weeks.

manas.q: When should pre-eclampsia without severe features be delivered?

children.note: PHOENIX trial: planned delivery cut maternal morbidity but increased neonatal unit admissions; decide case by case.

manas.q: What did the PHOENIX trial show about delivery at 34–37 weeks?

children.note: Stabilise mother first (BP, MgSO4), then deliver; <34 weeks, give steroids for fetal lungs if time allows.

manas.q: What is done before delivering a woman with severe pre-eclampsia?

children.note: Uncontrolled BP, eclampsia, pulmonary oedema, abruption, DIC, worsening HELLP or renal failure, fetal compromise.

manas.q: List indications for immediate delivery in pre-eclampsia.

children.note: Vaginal birth is often possible; caesarean is for usual obstetric reasons or rapid deterioration.

manas.q: Is caesarean section mandatory in pre-eclampsia?

children.note: ABC first, then magnesium, BP, delivery.
Call for help, left lateral position, clear airway, oxygen, protect from injury, IV access.

manas.q: What are the first steps when a pregnant woman fits?

children.note: Magnesium loading dose, control severe BP, monitor fetus; deliver once the mother is stable, never during a fit.

manas.q: When should a woman with eclampsia be delivered?

children.note: Epilepsy, hypoglycaemia, cerebral malaria, meningitis, stroke or cerebral venous thrombosis.

manas.q: List differentials of seizures in pregnancy.

children.note: Limit IV fluids (NICE: around 80 mL/hour) because capillary leak risks pulmonary oedema.

manas.q: Why are IV fluids restricted in severe pre-eclampsia?

children.note: Maternal and fetal.

manas.q: List maternal complications of pre-eclampsia.

children.note: Growth restriction, oligohydramnios, iatrogenic preterm birth, stillbirth.

manas.q: List fetal complications of pre-eclampsia.

children.note: Risk does not end at delivery.
BP often peaks 3–6 days postpartum, and eclampsia can still occur; keep monitoring and treating.

manas.q: When does postpartum BP often peak after pre-eclampsia?

children.note: Most resuscitations can be anticipated; preparation decides whether the first minute is used well.
Review maternal and fetal risk factors, agree who leads, who ventilates and who records time, and decide when to call extra help.

manas.q: What should a team agree on in a pre-birth briefing?

children.note: Warm towels, warm area, suction, self-inflating bag with term and preterm masks (sizes 1 and 0), stethoscope and a clock — tested before birth.

manas.q: Which equipment must be checked before every birth?

children.note: Birth switches the baby from placental to lung gas exchange within minutes.
The first breaths push fluid out of the airways and inflate the alveoli; failure to aerate the lungs is the core problem in most babies who need help.

manas.q: What is the key physiological problem in most babies needing resuscitation?

children.note: Lung aeration and oxygen relax pulmonary vessels, lung blood flow rises, and the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus begin to close.

manas.q: Why does pulmonary blood flow rise after the first breaths?

children.note: Healthy babies take several minutes (around 10) to reach normal oxygen saturation; early 'blue' colour is normal and colour is a poor guide.

manas.q: How quickly does oxygen saturation normalise after a healthy birth?

children.note: In primary apnoea stimulation may restart breathing; in secondary (terminal) apnoea only ventilation helps. They cannot be told apart at birth, so treat apnoea as secondary.

manas.q: Why is every apnoeic newborn treated as secondary apnoea?

children.note: Same core order everywhere: warm and dry, airway, breathing, circulation, drugs — reassessing heart rate after each step.
Dry thoroughly at birth and rub the back; remove the wet cloth. Drying is also the first stimulation.

manas.q: What is the first action for every newborn at birth?

children.note: A crying or well-breathing baby with good tone stays with the mother skin-to-skin, cord clamping deferred, monitored.

manas.q: What happens to a newborn who cries well at birth?

children.note: Head in neutral 'sniffing' position; suction mouth then nose only if secretions block the airway — routine suction is not advised.

manas.q: When should the newborn airway be suctioned?

children.note: If not breathing (or only gasping) after drying and clearing, start bag-mask ventilation; this is the single most important step.

manas.q: What is the single most important intervention in newborn resuscitation?

children.note: After about a minute of effective ventilation check HR: >100 continue care, 60–100 improve ventilation, <60 call for help and prepare advanced steps.

manas.q: How is heart rate used to guide the next resuscitation step?

children.note: Heart rate is the key sign; breathing and tone add context; colour and Apgar do not steer resuscitation.
Stethoscope over the chest is reliable in basic settings; cord pulsation can underestimate. Where available, ECG gives the fastest accurate HR.

manas.q: Which methods measure newborn heart rate and which is most accurate?

children.note: Look for crying or regular breaths; gasping is ineffective and must be treated like apnoea.

manas.q: How should gasping in a newborn be treated?

children.note: Apgar scores describe the baby at 1 and 5 minutes; do not wait for them before ventilating.

manas.q: Should you wait for the Apgar score before starting ventilation?

children.note: Chest rise and a rising heart rate prove ventilation works; if not, fix it before anything else.

children.topic: Start with air in term babies
children.note: Term and late-preterm babies start in room air; preterm babies start with low oxygen, adjusted to pre-ductal (right hand) oximetry.

manas.q: What oxygen concentration should term newborn resuscitation start with?

children.note: Mask adjust, Reposition head, Suction, Open mouth, Pressure increase, Alternative airway (laryngeal mask or tube).

manas.q: What does the MR SOPA mnemonic stand for?

children.note: Used when mask ventilation fails despite corrective steps, or before compressions in advanced settings; a laryngeal mask is an option from about 34 weeks.

manas.q: When is an alternative airway used in neonatal resuscitation?

children.note: Needed in only a small minority, and only after ventilation is effective.
HR stays below 60/min after at least 30 seconds of ventilation that moves the chest.

manas.q: When are chest compressions started in a newborn?

children.note: Two thumbs encircling the chest on the lower third of the sternum, depth about one-third of the chest; coordinate with breaths 3:1.

manas.q: Describe the preferred technique for neonatal chest compressions.

children.note: Increase inspired oxygen to 100% once compressions begin; wean by oximetry once HR recovers.

manas.q: What oxygen concentration is used during neonatal chest compressions?

children.note: Given if HR stays <60 despite effective ventilation and compressions; intravenous via umbilical vein or intraosseous is preferred over endotracheal.

manas.q: What is the preferred route for neonatal adrenaline?

children.note: Consider 10 mL/kg normal saline (or O-negative blood) over 5–10 min when blood loss or shock is suspected and HR does not respond.

manas.q: When is volume expansion given in neonatal resuscitation?

children.note: Timing of clamping is part of resuscitation.
For babies not needing immediate resuscitation, defer clamping for at least 60 seconds; it improves iron stores and blood volume.

manas.q: How long should cord clamping be deferred in a well newborn?

children.note: Intact cord milking is not advised in very preterm babies under 28 weeks (AHA) because of brain haemorrhage concerns.

manas.q: Why is cord milking avoided in babies under 28 weeks?

children.note: Cold stress raises oxygen use and mortality; overheating worsens brain injury.
Keep axillary temperature in the normal range; record it on admission as a quality marker.

manas.q: What is the target temperature range for a newborn?

children.note: Warm room, dry, remove wet cloth, skin-to-skin, hat, delay bathing; preterm babies under 32 weeks can go wet into a plastic bag under a radiant warmer.

manas.q: How are preterm babies kept warm at birth?

children.note: After asphyxia, fever is harmful to the brain; switch off warmers once temperature is normal.

manas.q: Why is hyperthermia avoided after birth asphyxia?

children.note: Approach depends on whether the baby is vigorous.
Routine care with the mother; no suction of mouth or trachea needed.

manas.q: How is a vigorous baby born through meconium managed?

children.note: Routine tracheal suction is no longer advised; start ventilation within the first minute, suctioning only if the airway seems blocked.

manas.q: Is routine tracheal suction recommended for a non-vigorous meconium baby?

children.note: Decided by the team leader and explained to the family.

children.topic: No heart rate despite all steps
children.note: AHA/ILCOR: if no HR after all steps, consider stopping around 20 minutes after birth, individualised to the situation.

manas.q: When does AHA guidance suggest considering stopping neonatal resuscitation?

children.note: HBB-style care without compressions or drugs: if no heart rate after about 10 minutes of effective ventilation, the baby has died. Follow your local protocol.

manas.q: In HBB-level care, when is a baby with no heart rate considered dead?

children.note: Failed gas exchange around birth causing hypoxaemia, hypercapnia and metabolic acidosis.
Evidence includes cord/early blood acidosis (pH <7.0 or large base deficit), low Apgar at 5–10 min, early encephalopathy and multi-organ injury.

manas.q: Which findings support a diagnosis of significant birth asphyxia?

children.note: Maternal (bleeding, eclampsia, hypotension), placental (abruption, insufficiency), cord (prolapse, tight knot), labour (obstruction, uterine rupture, shoulder dystocia), fetal (anaemia, infection).

manas.q: List causes of birth asphyxia by origin.

children.note: Encephalopathy graded mild, moderate or severe; grade sets prognosis and cooling eligibility.
Hyperalert, irritable, normal or brisk tone, dilated pupils, sympathetic signs, no seizures; usually settles within about 24 h.

manas.q: What are the features of Sarnat stage 1 HIE?

children.note: Lethargic, hypotonic, weak suck and Moro, constricted pupils, parasympathetic signs, seizures common.

manas.q: What are the features of Sarnat stage 2 HIE?

children.note: Stupor or coma, flaccid, absent primitive and often brainstem reflexes, irregular breathing; high death and disability.

manas.q: What are the features of Sarnat stage 3 HIE?

children.note: Blood is diverted to brain and heart, so other organs suffer.
Acute kidney injury with oliguria; watch urine output and creatinine.

manas.q: How does asphyxia affect the newborn kidney?

children.note: Myocardial dysfunction and hypotension; persistent pulmonary hypertension; meconium aspiration.

manas.q: Which cardiorespiratory complications follow birth asphyxia?

children.note: Raised liver enzymes, coagulopathy, low platelets, feed intolerance and risk of necrotising enterocolitis.

manas.q: Which liver, gut and blood problems follow asphyxia?

children.note: Hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia and hyponatraemia (often from inappropriate ADH).

manas.q: Which metabolic derangements follow birth asphyxia?

children.note: Supportive care prevents secondary brain injury.
Check early and often; both low and very high glucose worsen injury. Many protocols treat below 2.6 mmol/L; follow your local protocol.

manas.q: Why is glucose monitored closely after neonatal resuscitation?

children.note: Often subtle (lip smacking, cycling, apnoea, eye deviation); check glucose, calcium and sepsis; phenobarbital first line.

manas.q: What do subtle neonatal seizures look like?

children.note: Avoid fluid overload because of kidney injury and ADH excess; monitor urine output and weight; start feeds cautiously.

manas.q: Why are fluids restricted after birth asphyxia?

children.note: Temperature, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, perfusion, urine output and neurology; avoid both hypo- and hyperoxia.

manas.q: What should be monitored after neonatal resuscitation?

children.note: Cooling reduces death or disability in moderate–severe HIE in high-resource NICUs.
≥36 weeks, within 6 hours of birth, evidence of asphyxia (acidosis, low 10-min Apgar or ongoing resuscitation) plus moderate or severe encephalopathy.

manas.q: What are the usual criteria for therapeutic hypothermia?

children.note: Core temperature about 33.5 °C for 72 hours with full intensive care, then slow rewarming.

manas.q: What are the target temperature and duration of neonatal cooling?

children.note: The HELIX trial (2021, India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh) found cooling did not cut death or disability and raised deaths; do not cool without NICU support, protocols and follow-up.

manas.q: Why is therapeutic hypothermia controversial in low-resource settings?

children.note: Severity of encephalopathy is the strongest early guide.
Mild HIE usually has good outcome; moderate is variable; severe carries high death and cerebral palsy risk.

manas.q: How does Sarnat stage predict outcome?

children.note: MRI in the first 1–2 weeks showing basal ganglia/thalamic injury predicts poor motor outcome; all survivors need developmental follow-up.

manas.q: Which MRI pattern after HIE predicts poor motor outcome?

children.note: High-yield points examiners return to.

manas.q: What must be confirmed before starting neonatal compressions?

children.note: Reassess HR after each step; a rising HR is the best sign of success.

manas.q: Which sign drives each decision in neonatal resuscitation?

manas.q: Which algorithm style do Kenya's Basic Paediatric Protocols use?

manas.q: What does WHO basic newborn resuscitation emphasise?

children.note: Starts with five inflation breaths (longer, sustained) before regular ventilation breaths; AHA goes straight to PPV at 40–60/min.
